topics.intro: Simple harmonic motion is the back-and-forth motion of springs and pendulums. You will learn its defining equation, the speed and acceleration, periods of springs, pendulums and torsional systems, the energy changes, and how to combine sines and cosines.

sections.title: What simple harmonic motion is
body: **Simple harmonic motion (SHM)** is a back-and-forth motion in which the acceleration always points towards the centre (the equilibrium position) and is **proportional to the displacement:** **a = −ω²x.** The minus sign means the acceleration opposes the displacement. This one relationship is the test for SHM. A relation like a = −ω²x² or a = ωx does **not** describe SHM.

**The motion itself** is a sine or cosine: **x = A sin(ωt + φ).** A is the **amplitude** (the greatest displacement), ω is the **angular frequency** (rad/s), and φ is the **phase constant** (it says where the motion starts). The period is **T = 2π/ω** and the frequency is f = 1/T = ω/2π.

**Velocity and acceleration** come from differentiating: v = Aω cos(ωt + φ) and a = −Aω² sin(ωt + φ). So the **maximum speed is Aω** and the **maximum acceleration is Aω².** For x = −25 sin(3t + π/6) cm, A = 25 cm and ω = 3 rad/s, so v_max = 25 × 3 = **75 cm/s.** The minus sign in front does not change the size.
**Acceleration at a given moment.** For x = 5 cos(2t + π/6) cm, a = −ω²x = −4x. At t = 0, x = 5 cos 30° = 4.33 cm, so **a = −17.32 cm/s².** Always find x first, then multiply by −ω².

**Speed at a given displacement:** **v = ω√(A² − x²).** A block on a spring has amplitude 0.25 m and at x = 0.20 m its speed is 0.75 m/s. Then ω = 0.75/√(0.0625 − 0.04) = 0.75/0.15 = 5 rad/s and **T = 2π/5 = 1.256 s.** Another block with amplitude 0.35 m has speed 0.95 m/s at x = 0.25 m: ω = 0.95/√(0.1225 − 0.0625) = 0.95/0.245 = 3.88 rad/s, so **T = 1.62 s.**
**Amplitude is not the whole range.** If a clown's nose moves back and forth over a total distance of 0.42 m, that is the **peak-to-peak** distance. The amplitude is half of it: **0.21 m.**
keyPoints: SHM: a = −ω²x. Period T = 2π/ω.
v_max = Aω; a_max = Aω²; v = ω√(A² − x²).

sections.title: Periods of springs, pendulums and torsion oscillators
body: The period depends on the **system**, not on the amplitude. **Mass on a spring:** **T = 2π√(m/k)**, which depends on the mass m and the spring constant (restoring force constant) k. **Simple pendulum:** **T = 2π√(l/g)**, which depends only on the length and g. **Torsional oscillator** (a disc twisting on a wire): **T = 2π√(I/κ)**, which depends on the moment of inertia I and the torsion constant κ.

**What the period does not depend on:** the amplitude (for small swings) and, for a pendulum, the **mass.** A question that asks 'the period of SHM depends on which parameter?' has the answer 'the restoring force constant and the mass' for a spring system, not 'amplitude'.
**Natural angular frequency of a pendulum:** ω = 2π/T = **√(g/l).** For a spring, ω = √(k/m).

**Scaling.** A pendulum's period is 2 s. If both the mass and the length are doubled, the mass has no effect and the length doubling multiplies T by √2: T = 2√2 = **2.83 s.** If only the length were quadrupled, T would double to 4 s.
**A spring example.** A 0.5 kg mass on a spring with k = 200 N/m has T = 2π√(0.5/200) = **0.314 s.**

**Maximum speed from the period.** A 50 g mass vibrates with amplitude 12 cm and period 0.1 minutes. Convert first: 0.1 min = 6 s, so ω = 2π/6 = 1.047 rad/s. v_max = Aω = 0.12 × 1.047 = **0.126 m/s ≈ 0.13 m/s.** (The 50 g mass is not needed for this question.)
keyPoints: Spring: T = 2π√(m/k). Pendulum: T = 2π√(l/g). Torsion: T = 2π√(I/κ).

sections.title: Energy in SHM
body: The total energy of an SHM oscillator stays constant and shifts between kinetic and potential energy. For a spring with constant k: **total E = ½kA²**, **PE = ½kx²**, and **KE = ½k(A² − x²).** At the centre, all of E is kinetic. At the ends, all of it is potential.
**As a fraction of the maximum:** KE/KE_max = **1 − x²/A²** and PE/E = **x²/A².** The kinetic and potential fractions always add to 1.

**Finding the displacement for a given fraction.** If the kinetic energy is **2/5** of its maximum, then 1 − x²/A² = 2/5, so x²/A² = 3/5 and **x = A√(3/5) = 0.775A.** If instead the **potential** energy were 2/5 of the total, x²/A² = 2/5 and x = 0.632A. Always check which energy the question names.
**Half-way point.** KE = PE when x²/A² = 1/2, which gives x = A/√2 = 0.707A.
**Speed link.** Since KE = ½mv² and KE = ½k(A² − x²), you get v = √(k/m)·√(A² − x²) = ω√(A² − x²), the same formula as before.
keyPoints: E = ½kA²; PE = ½kx²; KE = ½k(A² − x²).

sections.title: Combining a sine and a cosine into one wave
body: A motion like **y = 6 cos 3t + 8 sin 3t** is still SHM with the same ω, but it can be written as one wave. Use y = R cos(3t − α) or y = R sin(3t + φ).
**Amplitude:** R = √(6² + 8²) = **10 m.** (Pythagoras on the two coefficients.)

**Phase constant.** In the cosine form, R cos(3t − α) = R cos α cos 3t + R sin α sin 3t, so R cos α = 6 and R sin α = 8. So tan α = 8/6 and **α = 53.13°.** In the sine form, R sin(3t + φ) = R sin φ cos 3t + R cos φ sin 3t gives R sin φ = 6 and R cos φ = 8, so tan φ = 6/8 and **φ = 36.87°.** Both describe the same motion. The answer '10 m with φ = 53°' uses the cosine form.
**Check.** At t = 0 the original gives y = 6. The cosine form gives 10 cos(−53.13°) = 10 × 0.6 = 6 ✓.
keyPoints: a cos θ + b sin θ has amplitude √(a² + b²).

topics.intro: Real oscillators lose energy, and driving them can make them swing hugely. This lesson covers damped motion, the three kinds of damping, decay and relaxation time, and forced oscillations and resonance.

sections.title: Damped oscillations: the three kinds
body: Real oscillators lose energy to friction or air resistance. This is **damping.** The damping force is **non-conservative:** it turns mechanical energy into heat, so the energy is not stored and returned.
The equation of motion is **m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = 0**, where m is the mass, b the damping constant and k the spring constant. The type of motion depends on how b² compares with **4mk**.

**Underdamped (light damping): b² < 4mk.** The system still oscillates, but the amplitude shrinks. **Critically damped: b² = 4mk.** The system returns to equilibrium as fast as possible without oscillating. **Overdamped (heavy damping): b² > 4mk.** The system returns to equilibrium slowly with no oscillation.

**Example.** For 3ẍ + 12ẋ + 39x = 0: m = 3, b = 12, k = 39. Then b² = 144 and 4mk = 468. Since 144 < 468, the motion is **underdamped.** For 4ẍ + 16ẋ + 16x = 0: b² = 256 and 4mk = 256, so it is **critically damped.**

**Car shock absorbers.** If the bonnet is pushed down and it does not bounce at all but slowly eases back, the damping is **overdamped.** A critically damped system would return quickly without bouncing.

**Reading the equation of motion.** x = x₀e^(−0.4t) cos ωt has a cosine, so it oscillates, and the exponential shrinks the amplitude slowly: **light damping.** If the equation is d²x/dt² = −16x, there is no damping term at all, so it is **SHM** with ω² = 16, ω = 4 rad/s and T = 2π/4 = **1.57 s.**
keyPoints: m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = 0.
b² < 4mk: underdamped. b² = 4mk: critical. b² > 4mk: overdamped.
Damping forces are non-conservative.

sections.title: Frequency, decay and relaxation time
body: **Natural (undamped) angular frequency:** **ω₀ = √(k/m).** For 2ẍ + 3ẋ + 5x = 12 sin(20t + φ), m = 2 and k = 5, so ω₀ = √(5/2) = **1.58 rad/s.** The number 20 in the driving term has nothing to do with the natural frequency.
**Damped frequency.** For light damping, the oscillation frequency is slightly lower: **ω_d = √(ω₀² − b²/(4m²)).** For m = 2, b = 4, k = 26: ω₀² = 13 and b²/(4m²) = 1, so ω_d = √12 = 3.46 rad/s.

**Decay of amplitude.** The amplitude falls as **A = A₀ e^(−t/τ)**, where τ is the **relaxation time.** A pendulum's amplitude falls from 0.05 m to 0.025 m in 5 minutes (300 s). Half the amplitude means e^(−300/τ) = 0.5, so 300/τ = ln 2 and **τ = 300/0.693 = 432.8 s.**
**Velocity at t = 0.** For x = 5e^(−0.75t) sin(ωt) with ω = 4: v = dx/dt = 5e^(−0.75t)[−0.75 sin ωt + ω cos ωt]. At t = 0, sin 0 = 0 and cos 0 = 1, so **v = 5 × 4 = 20 m/s.**

**Ways of describing a damped oscillator** include the logarithmic decrement, the relaxation time, the modulus of decay and the quality factor Q. All of these are standard, so a question asking which one is NOT used has the answer 'none of the above'.
keyPoints: ω₀ = √(k/m). ω_d = √(ω₀² − b²/(4m²)).
Amplitude: A = A₀e^(−t/τ).
Relaxation time for a halving amplitude: τ = t/ln 2.

sections.title: Forced oscillations and resonance
body: A **forced oscillation** has a driving force added: m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = F₀ cos(ωt + φ). **The driving angular frequency is the coefficient of t** inside the cosine or sine. For 3ẍ + 6ẋ + 14x = 120 cos(20t + φ), the driving frequency is **20 rad/s.** It is given directly.

**Resonance** is the large build-up of amplitude when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency. When the driving frequency coincides with the natural undamped frequency, **resonance** is most likely (not beats, the Doppler effect or an echo).

**With damping, the amplitude peaks slightly below ω₀:** **ω_res = √(k/m − b²/(2m²)).** For 2ẍ + 3ẋ + 7x = 4 cos(ωt + φ): k/m = 3.5 and b²/(2m²) = 9/8 = 1.125, so ω_res = √2.375 = **1.54 rad/s.** For 5ẍ + 7ẋ + 9x = 8 sin(πt): k/m = 1.8 and b²/(2m²) = 49/50 = 0.98, so ω_res = √0.82 = **0.91 rad/s.** Be careful here: √1.8 = 1.34 is the value without the damping correction, not the answer.

**Mechanical impedance.** For a driven oscillator, **Z = √(b² + (mω − k/ω)²).** For 3ẍ + 7ẋ + 10x = 10 sin(20t + φ): mω = 60 and k/ω = 0.5, so Z = √(49 + 59.5²) = 59.91 (in mechanical ohms, kg/s). Per unit mass, **Z/m = 59.91/3 = 19.97.**
**Everyday resonance:** pushing a swing at its natural frequency; a bridge shaking when marchers step in time; a radio tuned to a station.
keyPoints: The driving frequency is the number multiplying t.

topics.intro: Waves carry energy, and sound is the wave we use every day. This lesson covers wave basics, waves on strings, the speed of sound, pipes and resonance tubes, the Doppler effect, and beats and interference.

sections.title: Wave basics: speed, frequency and wavelength
body: A **wave** carries energy without carrying matter along. **Transverse** waves shake the medium at right angles to the direction of travel (waves on a string). **Longitudinal** waves shake it along the direction of travel (sound: compressions and rarefactions). Light and radio are **electromagnetic** waves, which need no medium and can carry data, voice and video across the world.

**The key relationships:** **v = fλ**, **T = 1/f**, **ω = 2πf** and the **wave number k = 2π/λ.** So v = ω/k. A clothesline shaken at 2.00 Hz with wave speed 12.0 m/s has T = 0.5 s, λ = 12/2 = 6 m and k = 2π/6 = **1.05 rad/m.**

**Reading the wave equation.** For y = A sin(ωt − kx), the wave moves in the **+x** direction at speed **v = ω/k.** For y = 6 sin(7πt − 0.04πx + π/6): ω = 7π and k = 0.04π, so **v = 175 m/s.** For **y = 5 sin(2πx − 3πt)** (x in cm), k = 2π and ω = 3π, so v = 3π/2π = **1.5 cm/s**. The form sin(kx − ωt) is the same wave as −sin(ωt − kx), and it travels in the **+x direction.** A wave with (ωt + kx) travels in the −x direction.
**Particle acceleration.** The particles of the medium move in SHM, so a = −ω²y. For Y = 0.5 sin(0.1x − 0.4t), ω = 0.4, so **a = −0.16 Y.**

**Wave speed from a boat.** A boat takes 3.20 s to go from its highest to lowest point. That is half a period, so T = 6.40 s. The crests are 7.50 m apart, so λ = 7.50 m and v = λ/T = 7.50/6.40 = **1.172 m/s.**

**Phase difference and wavelength.** A phase difference of 360° is one wavelength, so 90° is λ/4. If two points 0.72 m apart differ by 90°, λ = 4 × 0.72 = 2.88 m and v = fλ = 60 × 2.88 = **172.8 m/s** (for a 60 Hz wave). For points 60 cm apart at 50 Hz: λ = 2.40 m and v = **120 m/s.**
**When a wave enters a new medium,** its **frequency stays the same** (it is set by the source). Its speed and wavelength change together, since v = fλ.
keyPoints: v = fλ = ω/k. k = 2π/λ.
sin(kx − ωt) moves in +x; sin(ωt + kx) moves in −x.

sections.title: Waves on strings
body: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is **v = √(T/μ)**, where T is the **tension** and **μ is the mass per unit length** (kg/m). A tighter or lighter string gives a faster wave.

**Example.** A string is 5 m long with a mass of 0.01 kg and a tension of 10 N. μ = 0.01/5 = 0.002 kg/m, so v = √(10/0.002) = **70.7 m/s.** Another: a string 34.5 cm long with a mass of 6.9 g has μ = 0.0069/0.345 = 0.02 kg/m, so at 10 N v = √(10/0.02) = **22.4 m/s.** Convert grams and centimetres to kilograms and metres first.

**A hanging rope.** A 2.00 kg rope hangs down an 80.0 m shaft with a 20 kg box at the bottom. T ≈ 20g, and μ = 2.00/80.0 = 0.025 kg/m. With g = 10, T = 200 N and **v = √(200/0.025) = 89.4 m/s.** With g = 9.8 it is 88.5 m/s, so the closest answer is chosen.
**A round trip.** A 550 m wire with a mass of 1 kg is under 45 N. μ = 1/550, so v = √(45 × 550) = 157.3 m/s. A pulse goes to the far end and back (1100 m) in 1100/157.3 = **6.99 s.**

**A string fixed at both ends** vibrates in standing waves. The **fundamental** has half a wavelength on the string: λ = 2L, so **f₁ = v/(2L).** The harmonics are f₂ = 2f₁, f₃ = 3f₁, and so on. The **first overtone** is the **second harmonic**, 2f₁. A piano wire 0.5 m long with a mass of 0.01 kg at 800 N: μ = 0.02, v = 200 m/s and f₁ = 200/(2 × 0.5) = **200 Hz.** A string of length 50 cm with wave speed 335 m/s has f₁ = 335 Hz, so its first overtone is **670 Hz.**
**Finding tension.** T = μv². A violin string of 0.5 m with μ = 4 g/m and f₁ = 200 Hz has v = 2Lf = 200 m/s, so **T = 0.004 × 200² = 160 N.**

**Frequency and tension.** For the same string, f ∝ √T. So the tension ratio is the square of the frequency ratio: strings at 300 Hz and 450 Hz have T_Y/T_X = (450/300)² = **2.25.** A sonometer wire at 10 N sounding 250 Hz needs 10 × (350/250)² = **19.6 N** to sound 350 Hz.
**Nodes on a fixed string.** A string fixed at x = 0 carries a 440 Hz wave at 143 m/s, so λ = 143/440 = 0.325 m. Nodes are half a wavelength apart: at **0, 0.1625 m and 0.325 m.**
keyPoints: v = √(T/μ), with μ in kg/m.
Fixed string: f₁ = v/(2L); harmonics n f₁; first overtone = 2f₁.

sections.title: The speed of sound
body: Sound is a **longitudinal** wave. Its speed depends on the medium. In a fluid, **v = √(B/ρ)**, where B is the **bulk modulus** and ρ the density. These two are the only properties that matter. In air, the speed rises with temperature: **v = v₀√(T/T₀)**, where T is in kelvin. About 331 m/s at 0 °C.

**Examples.** At 25 °C (298.15 K): v = 331√(298.15/273.15) = **346 m/s.** If the speed is 332 m/s at 0 °C, then at 30 °C it is 332√(303.15/273.15) = **350 m/s.** Always convert to kelvin before using the ratio.
**Thunder.** Light arrives almost instantly, so the delay in the thunder is the travel time of the sound. A 2 s delay at 330 m/s means **660 m** away.

**Echoes.** An echo travels there and back. A pulse sent down at 200 m/s that returns after 1.2 s from one layer and after 1.4 s from another has gone to depths of 200 × 1.2/2 = 120 m and 200 × 1.4/2 = 140 m. The layers are **20 m** apart.
**Sound across a boundary:** the frequency does not change. The speed and wavelength do.
keyPoints: v = √(B/ρ) in fluids; v ∝ √T (in kelvin) in air.
Echo distance = speed × time/2.
The frequency of a wave does not change at a boundary.

Which statement is true when a wave goes from one medium into another?
exercises.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source.

sections.title: Pipes, resonance tubes and end corrections
body: Air in a pipe vibrates in standing waves. **A closed pipe** (one end shut) has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. Its fundamental has a quarter of a wavelength in the pipe: **L = λ/4, so f₁ = v/(4L)**, and only **odd harmonics** exist (f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁, …). **An open pipe** (both ends open) has antinodes at both ends: **L = λ/2, f₁ = v/(2L)**, and it has all harmonics.
**Closed-pipe examples.** If f₁ = 170 Hz and v = 340 m/s, then L = v/(4f) = 340/680 = **0.5 m.** A pipe closed at one end with fundamental 220 Hz and v = 345 m/s has L = 345/880 = **0.39 m.**

**Temperature.** A closed pipe of length 0.35 m at 27 °C: v = 331√(300/273) = 347 m/s, so f₁ = 347/(4 × 0.35) = **247 Hz.** The next two overtones are the odd harmonics 3f₁ = **741 Hz** and 5f₁ = **1235 Hz.**

**Resonance tube.** A tuning fork is held over a tube of water and the water level changes. The **first** resonance is when the air column is a quarter wavelength: **λ = 4L.** With a 250 Hz fork and L = 0.3 m: λ = 1.2 m and v = fλ = **300 m/s.** With 480 Hz and L = 0.20 m: λ = 0.80 m and v = **384 m/s.**

**End correction.** The antinode sits slightly **beyond** the open end. So the effective length is longer than the real length. For an open pipe 15 cm long with an antinode 0.5 cm outside each end, L_eff = 15 + 2(0.5) = 16 cm = 0.16 m, and with f₁ = 200 Hz, **v = 2 f L_eff = 2 × 200 × 0.16 = 64 m/s.**
keyPoints: Closed pipe: f₁ = v/(4L), odd harmonics. Open pipe: f₁ = v/(2L), all harmonics.
Resonance tube: λ = 4L at the first resonance.
Add the end correction to the length.

example.problem: Find the fundamental frequency of an open pipe 0.5 m long. (v = 340 m/s)

exercises.prompt: What is the length of a closed organ pipe with a fundamental of 170 Hz when the speed of sound is 340 m/s?
A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental of 220 Hz. If v = 345 m/s, how long is the pipe?
In a resonance tube, a 250 Hz fork gives the first resonance at an air column of 0.3 m. What is the speed of sound?
A resonance tube has a first-resonance air column of 20 cm with a 480 Hz fork. Neglecting end effects, find v.
An open pipe is 15 cm long with fundamental 200 Hz and antinodes 0.5 cm beyond each end. Find the speed of sound.

exercises.explanation: v = 347 m/s, f₁ = 247 Hz, then 3f₁ and 5f₁. A closed pipe has only odd harmonics.

sections.title: The Doppler effect
body: When the source or the observer moves, the frequency you hear changes. **General formula:** **f′ = f (v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s)**, where v is the speed of sound, v_o the observer's speed and v_s the source's speed. **Rule:** things moving **towards** each other raise the pitch, and things moving **apart** lower it. So **the observer moving towards the source adds v_o on top** and **the source moving towards the observer subtracts v_s from the bottom.**
**Observer moving towards a still source.** A 500 Hz siren, v = 340 m/s, you drive towards it at 20 m/s: f′ = 500 × (340 + 20)/340 = **529 Hz.**

**Source moving towards a still observer.** A fire engine at 20 m/s with a 500 Hz siren, approaching a parked car: f′ = 500 × 340/(340 − 20) = **531 Hz.** The standard formula is f₀ = f_s/(1 − v_s/v). Note the difference from the previous case: 529 Hz and 531 Hz are similar but not equal.

**Both moving towards each other.** Two trains at 16.6 m/s and 12.5 m/s approach, and a whistle of 512 Hz is on the first: f′ = 512 × (340 + 12.5)/(340 − 16.6) = **558 Hz.** If the whistle were 600 Hz: 600 × 352.5/323.4 = **654 Hz.** Use the right frequency in the formula.
**Both moving apart.** Cars at 18 m/s (source) and 15 m/s (observer) moving apart with a 550 Hz whistle: f′ = 550 × (340 − 15)/(340 + 18) = **499 Hz.**

**A passing truck.** A truck at 96 km/h (26.67 m/s) sounds a 400 Hz horn. Just after it passes you, the source is moving away: f′ = 400 × 346/(346 + 26.67) = **371 Hz.** Always convert km/h to m/s first.
keyPoints: Towards: higher pitch. Apart: lower pitch.
f′ = f(v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s).
Convert km/h to m/s and use the source's own frequency.

example.problem: A 1000 Hz source moves away from a stationary listener at 10 m/s (v = 340). What is the frequency heard?

exercises.prompt: A 500 Hz siren sounds and you drive towards it at 20 m/s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What frequency do you hear?
A fire engine's siren is 500 Hz and it approaches a stationary car at 20 m/s. What does the person in the car hear?
Two trains approach at 16.6 m/s and 12.5 m/s. A 512 Hz whistle sounds on the first. What does the observer on the second hear?
Two trains approach at 16.6 m/s and 12.5 m/s. A 600 Hz whistle sounds on one. What does the observer on the other train hear?
Two cars move apart at 18 m/s and 15 m/s. A 550 Hz whistle sounds. What does the other driver hear?
A truck at 96 km/h sounds a 400 Hz horn (v = 346 m/s). What does a person hear just after it has passed?
Which relation gives the frequency heard by a stationary observer when a source approaches at v_s?
exercises.explanation: The wavelength ahead of the source is shortened, giving f/(1 − v_s/v).

sections.title: Beats, standing waves and interference
body: **Beats.** Two notes of close frequencies make the loudness rise and fall. The **beat frequency** is the **difference** of the frequencies: f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|, and the beat **period** is 1/f_beat. For 300 Hz and 298 Hz: f_beat = 2 Hz and the beat period is **0.5 s.**

**Standing waves** form when two waves of the **same frequency and amplitude** travel in **opposite directions.** Points of zero displacement are **nodes**, and points of maximum displacement are **antinodes.** Nodes and antinodes belong to **standing waves.** For example, y₁ = A sin(ωt + kx) and y₃ = A sin(ωt − kx) travel in opposite directions and combine into a standing wave. Note that y₂ = −A sin(ωt + kx) and y₄ = −A sin(ωt − kx) also travel in opposite directions, so that pair gives a standing wave too.

**Interference of two sources.** Two identical speakers in phase give **destructive interference** where the path difference is **half a wavelength** (or 3λ/2, and so on). For 1550 Hz and v = 320 m/s, λ = 320/1550 = 0.2065 m, so the first dip occurs at a path difference of λ/2 = 0.1032 m.

**A geometry problem.** A listener is 12 m from one speaker, on a line perpendicular to the line joining the speakers. The second speaker is a distance d to the side. The path difference is √(12² + d²) − 12 = 0.1032, so √(144 + d²) = 12.1032, giving d² = 2.488 and **d = 1.58 m.** (The nearest option is chosen.) This is the smallest non-zero separation that gives silence at that point.
**Constructive interference** needs a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths: 0, λ, 2λ, …
keyPoints: f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|.
Standing wave: two equal waves in opposite directions; nodes and antinodes.
Destructive interference: path difference λ/2, 3λ/2, …

example.problem: Two sources produce 440 Hz and 444 Hz. How many beats are heard in 10 s?

exercises.prompt: Two tones have frequencies of 300 Hz and 298 Hz. What is the beat period?
exercises.explanation: f_beat = 2 Hz, so the period is 0.5 s.

exercises.prompt: Antinodes and nodes occur in:
exercises.explanation: They are features of standing waves.

exercises.prompt: What path difference gives destructive interference for two in-phase sources?
exercises.explanation: A half-wavelength difference puts the waves in antiphase.

exercises.prompt: Two in-phase speakers emit 1550 Hz (v = 320 m/s). What is the first path difference that gives silence?
A guitar string is fixed at x = 0 and carries 440 Hz at 143 m/s. Where are the first three nodes?
exercises.explanation: λ = 0.325 m, and nodes are λ/2 apart: 0, 0.1625 m, 0.325 m.

topics.intro: Mirrors form images by reflection. This lesson gives you the mirror equation with its sign convention, the five concave-mirror cases, the behaviour of convex and plane mirrors, and the worked patterns that appear in the question bank: erect-image problems, the plane-mirror height rule and spherical aberration.

sections.title: The mirror equation and sign convention
body: A **concave mirror** curves inwards like the inside of a spoon and is **converging**. A **convex mirror** curves outwards and is **diverging**. A spherical mirror has a **centre of curvature C** at distance **R** (the radius of curvature), and a **focal point F** halfway between the mirror and C: **f = R/2.**

**The mirror equation** is **1/f = 1/u + 1/v.** Here u is the object distance, v the image distance, and f the focal length. The **magnification** is **m = −v/u** (the image height divided by the object height; a negative m means the image is inverted).

**Sign convention used in this course:** distances to **real** objects and **real images** (in front of the mirror) are **positive**; a **virtual** image (behind the mirror) has **negative v**. A **concave** mirror has **positive f**; a **convex** mirror has **negative f**. With this convention, if m comes out positive the image is erect, and if it is negative the image is inverted.

**Worked pattern.** Write down f (from R/2 if the radius is given), write u, then solve 1/v = 1/f − 1/u. Do not forget the last step: **v = 1/(1/f − 1/u).** The most common slip is to stop at 1/v and quote that as the answer.

**Real or virtual?** A positive v means the image is real and in front of the mirror, and it can be caught on a screen. A negative v means the image is virtual and appears behind the mirror, and it cannot be put on a screen.
keyPoints: Real image: v positive. Virtual image: v negative.
Concave mirror: f positive. Convex mirror: f negative.
Always invert 1/v at the end to get v.

example.problem: An object is placed 2 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius 8 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.
steps: f = R/2 = 4 cm and u = 2 cm.
example.answer: The image is 4 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect and twice the size of the object.

exercises.prompt: A concave mirror has radius of curvature R = 12 cm. An object is placed 3 cm in front of it. Where is the image and what is it like?
options: 6 cm behind the mirror, virtual and erect
6 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
2 cm behind the mirror, virtual and erect
2 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
exercises.explanation: f = R/2 = 6 cm. 1/v = 1/6 − 1/3 = −1/6, so v = −6 cm: the image is 6 cm behind the mirror (virtual). m = −v/u = 6/3 = +2, so it is erect and twice the size. The object is inside the focal length, which always gives a virtual, erect, magnified image in a concave mirror.
exercises.hint: First find f from R. Then check whether u is smaller than f.

exercises.prompt: A concave mirror has focal length 10 cm. An object is placed 30 cm from it. Find the image distance and the magnification.
exercises.explanation: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so v = 15 cm (real). m = −v/u = −15/30 = −0.5: inverted and half the size.

exercises.prompt: A concave mirror has radius of curvature 40 cm. An object stands 50 cm in front of it. What is the image distance?
exercises.explanation: f = R/2 = 20 cm. 1/v = 1/20 − 1/50 = 3/100, so v = 100/3 = 33.3 cm, a real image in front of the mirror. The object is beyond C (50 cm > 40 cm), so the image is real, inverted and smaller (m = −33.3/50 = −0.67).
exercises.hint: Remember f = R/2 before using the equation.

exercises.prompt: A candle flame is 40 cm from a concave mirror of radius 64 cm. Which description of the image is correct?
options: Real, inverted, 160 cm from the mirror
Virtual, erect, 150 cm behind the mirror
Real, inverted, 30 cm from the mirror
Real, inverted, 120 cm from the mirror
exercises.explanation: f = 32 cm. 1/v = 1/32 − 1/40 = (5 − 4)/160 = 1/160, so v = 160 cm, positive, so the image is real and in front of the mirror. m = −160/40 = −4: inverted and four times larger. The object lies between F (32 cm) and C (64 cm).
exercises.hint: Compute 1/32 − 1/40 with a common denominator of 160.

sections.title: Images in concave and convex mirrors
body: **Concave mirror, five cases** (object distance u compared with f and R = 2f):

**1. Beyond C (u > 2f):** the image is **real, inverted, diminished,** between F and C. **2. At C (u = 2f):** the image is **real, inverted, the same size,** and also at C. **3. Between F and C (f < u < 2f):** the image is **real, inverted, magnified,** beyond C. For f = 10 cm and u = 15 cm, 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm and m = −2. **4. At F (u = f):** the image forms at infinity. **5. Inside F (u < f):** the image is **virtual, erect, magnified,** behind the mirror. This is how a shaving or make-up mirror works.

**Convex mirror:** the image is **always virtual, erect and diminished,** whatever the object distance. It lies between the mirror and its focal point. This wide field of view is why convex mirrors are used as shop security mirrors and car wing mirrors. Example: a convex mirror gives an image one third the size of an object 18 cm away. m = −v/u = 1/3 gives v = −6 cm; then 1/f = 1/18 − 1/6 = −1/9, so **f = −9 cm.**

**Using the magnification to find the object distance.** If the image is erect and magnified 2 times in a concave mirror of f = 12 cm, then m = 2 means v = −2u. Substituting: 1/12 = 1/u − 1/(2u) = 1/(2u), so **u = 6 cm** and v = −12 cm. The object is inside the focal length, as an erect magnified image needs.

**Erect-image problems with a given separation.** For an erect (virtual) image magnified m times, the image is behind the mirror at v = −mu. The object-to-image distance is u + mu = (1 + m)u. For m = 4 with the image 32 cm from the object: 5u = 32, so u = 6.4 cm and v = −25.6 cm. Then 1/f = 1/6.4 − 1/25.6 = 0.1172, so **f = 8.53 cm** (6.4 cm is the object distance, not the focal length). For m = 3.5 with a separation of 3.5 cm: 4.5u = 3.5, u = 0.778 cm, v = −2.72 cm and **f = 1.089 cm.**

**Given v and R.** A virtual image 12 cm from a concave mirror of radius 120 cm (f = 60 cm): 1/u = 1/f − 1/v = 1/60 + 1/12 = 6/60, so **u = 10 cm.** The object is inside the focal length, as it must be for an upright image.
keyPoints: Concave: beyond C real, inverted, smaller; at C same size; between F and C magnified; inside F virtual, erect, magnified.
Convex: always virtual, erect and diminished.
Erect and magnified m times: v = −mu.
Check every answer against the object position.

exercises.prompt: An object is placed 15 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Which statement is correct?
options: Real, inverted, magnified, image 30 cm from the mirror
Real, inverted, diminished, image 6 cm from the mirror
Virtual, erect, magnified, image 30 cm behind the mirror
Real, inverted, same size, image 15 cm from the mirror
exercises.explanation: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm, positive (real). m = −30/15 = −2: inverted and twice as large. The object is between F (10 cm) and C (20 cm).
exercises.hint: Compare u = 15 cm with f = 10 cm and R = 20 cm.

exercises.prompt: The image formed by a convex mirror is always:
exercises.explanation: A convex mirror is diverging. The reflected rays never meet, so the image can only be virtual, formed behind the mirror, erect and smaller than the object.

exercises.prompt: A convex mirror forms an image one third the size of an object placed 18 cm from it. Find its focal length.
exercises.explanation: m = −v/u = 1/3, so v = −6 cm. 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/18 − 1/6 = −2/18, so f = −9 cm. A convex mirror always has negative f.
exercises.hint: The image is virtual, so v is negative.

exercises.prompt: A concave mirror of focal length 12 cm forms an erect image twice the size of the object. How far is the object from the mirror?
exercises.explanation: Erect and magnified 2 times means v = −2u. Then 1/12 = 1/u − 1/(2u) = 1/(2u), so u = 6 cm, and v = −12 cm. The object is inside F (6 cm < 12 cm).
exercises.hint: Write v in terms of u, then substitute into 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

exercises.prompt: A spherical mirror forms an erect image four times the height of the object, and the object and image are 32 cm apart. What is the focal length of the mirror?
exercises.explanation: Erect and four times larger means v = −4u. The image is behind the mirror and the object is in front, so the separation is u + 4u = 5u = 32 cm, giving u = 6.4 cm and v = −25.6 cm. Then 1/f = 1/6.4 − 1/25.6 = 0.1172, so f = 8.53 cm. The 6.4 cm option is the object distance.
exercises.hint: Do not stop at u = 6.4 cm: that is not f.

exercises.prompt: An erect image is formed 12 cm behind a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 120 cm. Where is the object?
exercises.hint: v is negative for a virtual image.

exercises.prompt: Which statements are true about a concave mirror? (i) An object beyond C gives a real, inverted, diminished image. (ii) An object between F and C gives a real, inverted, magnified image. (iii) An object at C gives a real, inverted image the same size. (iv) An object inside F gives a virtual, erect, magnified image.
exercises.explanation: All four statements are the standard results for a concave mirror, so all are true.

sections.title: Plane mirrors and aberration
body: **A plane mirror** has infinite radius, so the equation gives v = −u: the image is **virtual, erect, the same size,** and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Someone standing 2 m from the mirror sees their image 4 m away from them.

**Smallest full-length mirror.** To see your whole body you need a mirror only **half your height.** For someone 1.8 m tall, the minimum mirror is **0.9 m**, and for 1.7 m it is 0.85 m. The mirror must be placed so that its top edge is halfway between the eye and the top of the head, and its bottom edge halfway between the eye and the feet. The distance from the mirror does not matter.

**Spherical aberration** happens when rays far from the optical axis of a spherical mirror or lens come to a focus at a different point from rays near the axis, so the image is blurred. Using only a small aperture, or a **parabolic** mirror, reduces it. **Chromatic aberration** is a different fault: it happens only in lenses, because different colours refract by different amounts. Mirrors do not have it, because reflection does not depend on wavelength.
keyPoints: Plane mirror: image virtual, erect, same size, v = −u.
Minimum full-length mirror = half the person's height.
Spherical aberration: marginal rays focus elsewhere; chromatic aberration: only in lenses.

exercises.prompt: A woman 1.7 m tall wants to see her whole body in a vertical plane mirror. What is the minimum height of the mirror?
exercises.explanation: The mirror needs to be half the person's height: 1.7/2 = 0.85 m. This does not depend on how far she stands from it.
exercises.hint: Think of the two edges as halfway points.

exercises.prompt: A person stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is the person from the image?
exercises.explanation: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front (2 m), so the person-to-image distance is 2 + 2 = 4 m.

exercises.prompt: The blurring that occurs because rays far from the axis of a spherical mirror or lens focus at a different point from rays near the axis is called:
exercises.explanation: This is spherical aberration. Chromatic aberration comes from colours refracting by different amounts, and myopia and astigmatism are eye defects.

exercises.prompt: Which optical fault cannot occur in a mirror?
exercises.explanation: Reflection does not depend on wavelength, so a mirror has no chromatic aberration. Lenses do, because the refractive index of glass depends on colour.

topics.intro: Light changes direction and speed when it enters a new medium. This lesson covers Snell’s law and relative index, the critical angle and apparent depth, thin lenses, the lensmaker’s equation and lens power, defects of the eye, and prisms with dispersion and achromatic lenses.

sections.title: Refraction and Snell’s law
body: **Refraction** is the bending of light when it passes from one medium into another because its speed changes. The **refractive index** of a medium is **n = c/v**, where c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Glass with n = 1.5 slows light to 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s, and water with n = 1.33 to about 2.26 × 10⁸ m/s. A medium with a higher n is **optically denser,** and it slows light more.

**Snell’s law:** **n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂,** with both angles measured from the **normal**. Going into a denser medium the ray bends **towards** the normal; going into a less dense medium it bends **away.** A ray of 30° in air entering glass (n = 1.5) has sin θ₂ = sin 30°/1.5, so θ₂ = 19.5°, and the reverse path out of glass at 30° gives sin θ = 1.5 × 0.5, so θ = 48.6°.

**Relative refractive index.** The index of medium 2 relative to medium 1 is **ₙ₁n₂ = n₂/n₁.** If water relative to air is 1.55 and oil relative to air is 1.73, then water relative to oil is **1.55/1.73 = 0.90.** If glass relative to water is 7:5 and glass relative to air is 5:3, then water relative to air is (5/3)/(7/5) = **25:21.**

**What changes and what does not.** When light refracts, its **frequency stays constant** because it is set by the source. Its **speed and wavelength both change,** because v = fλ and f is fixed. So in a denser medium light travels slower and has a shorter wavelength.
**Reflection and energy.** In reflection the energy is conserved; at a perfect reflector all the light is reflected and there is no refraction.
keyPoints: n = c/v; denser medium means higher n and slower light.
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ (angles from the normal).
Relative index: n₂/n₁; divide ratios to make the common medium cancel.
Frequency is constant; speed and wavelength change.

example.problem: The index of glass relative to water is 7:5 and glass relative to air is 5:3. Find the index of water relative to air.

exercises.prompt: The refractive index of water relative to air is 1.55 and that of oil relative to air is 1.73. What is the refractive index of water relative to oil?
exercises.explanation: Water relative to oil = n(water/air) ÷ n(oil/air) = 1.55/1.73 = 0.896 ≈ 0.90. The 1.12 option is the inverse (oil relative to water).
exercises.hint: Which medium is the 'to' and which is the 'from'?

exercises.prompt: The refractive index of glass relative to water is 7:5, and of glass relative to air is 5:3. What is the index of water relative to air?
exercises.explanation: Water/air = (glass/air) ÷ (glass/water) = (5/3) ÷ (7/5) = 25/21. The glass index cancels.
exercises.hint: Divide the two ratios so the glass cancels.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about refracted light is correct? (i) The speed is unchanged. (ii) The frequency remains constant. (iii) The wavelength remains constant.
exercises.explanation: Only the frequency is constant. Speed and wavelength both change together (v = fλ with f fixed), so (i) and (iii) are false.

exercises.prompt: A ray of light in air hits glass (n = 1.5) at 30° to the normal. What is the angle of refraction?
exercises.explanation: sin θ₂ = sin 30°/1.5 = 0.333, so θ₂ = 19.5°. The ray bends towards the normal in the denser medium. The 48.6° option is for light going out of the glass.
exercises.hint: Going into glass means the angle gets smaller.

sections.title: Critical angle, total reflection and apparent depth
body: **Critical angle.** When light goes from a denser medium (n₁) to a less dense one (n₂), the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the **critical angle θc** the refracted ray skims along the boundary (90°). So **sin θc = n₂/n₁.** For light leaving water into air, θc = sin⁻¹(1/1.33) = **48.75°.** For glass of n = 1.5 into air it is 41.8°.

**General case:** for n₁ = 1.89 and n₂ = 1.33, θc = sin⁻¹(1.33/1.89) = **44.7°.** If the angle of incidence is bigger than θc there is **total internal reflection:** all the light is reflected. This is how optical fibres and prisms in binoculars work.

**A diver and the critical angle.** A diver beneath still water (n = 1.33) wants a beam to just reach someone on a distant bank, so the beam must leave the surface almost along the water. The beam must hit the surface at the critical angle, **48.8°** to the normal. The depth of the diver (here 3.5 m) does not change this angle.

**Finding n from θc.** From sin θc = 1/n, we get n = 1/sin θc. If θc = 45°, then n = 1/0.7071 = **√2 = 1.414.** A ray in this liquid at 30° incidence to air gives sin θ = 1.414 × 0.5 = 0.7071, so θ = **45°.** In the same way, with θc = 52.7° the index is about 1.26 and a 40° ray emerges at about 54°.

**Apparent depth.** Viewed from directly above, an object under water seems closer to the surface: **apparent depth = real depth/n.** A pool 1.6 m deep (n = 1.33) looks **1.2 m** deep. A fish at 2.4 m seems to be at 1.8 m.
keyPoints: sin θc = n₂/n₁ (from denser to less dense).
Beyond θc there is total internal reflection.
n = 1/sin θc for a medium against air.
Apparent depth = real depth/n.

exercises.prompt: What is the critical angle for light going from water (n = 1.33) to air?
exercises.explanation: sin θc = 1/1.33 = 0.752, so θc = 48.75° ≈ 48.8°. The 41.8° option is for glass (n = 1.5).
exercises.hint: θc = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁).

exercises.prompt: The critical angle for light passing from a material of n₁ = 1.89 to a material of n₂ = 1.33 is:
exercises.hint: The denser medium is in the denominator.

exercises.prompt: A diver 3.5 m beneath still water (n = 1.33) shines a beam towards the surface so that a person on a distant bank can just see it. At what angle to the normal must the beam hit the surface?
exercises.explanation: The beam must reach the surface at the critical angle, sin⁻¹(1/1.33) = 48.75° ≈ 48.8°. The depth is a distraction.
exercises.hint: Which angle lets light only just escape?

exercises.prompt: A liquid has critical angle 45° at its boundary with air. A ray in the liquid hits the surface at 30°. At what angle does it emerge into the air?
exercises.hint: Find n from the critical angle first.

exercises.prompt: A swimming pool is 1.6 m deep and the water has n = 1.33. How deep does the bottom appear when viewed from directly above?
exercises.explanation: Apparent depth = real depth/n = 1.6/1.33 = 1.2 m. The pool looks shallower than it is.
exercises.hint: Apparent depth is smaller than real depth.

sections.title: Thin lenses and image formation
body: **A converging (convex) lens** is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays together at a focus; its **f is positive.** A **diverging (concave) lens** is thinner in the middle and spreads rays out; its **f is negative.** The thin lens equation has the same form as the mirror equation: **1/f = 1/u + 1/v,** with **m = −v/u.** Real images have positive v and virtual images have negative v.

**Converging lens, image formation by object position.** **Beyond 2f:** image **real, inverted, diminished,** between f and 2f, closer to the lens than the object. **At 2f:** real, inverted, same size, at 2f. **Between f and 2f:** real, inverted, magnified, beyond 2f. **At f:** image at infinity. **Inside f (u < f):** virtual, erect, magnified. A **magnifying glass** is exactly this last case, so the object must be placed **less than one focal length** away.

**Worked examples.** An object 5 cm tall stands 60 cm from a lens of f = 20 cm: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/60 = 1/30, so **v = 30 cm.** The magnification is −30/60 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and **2.5 cm** tall. For an object at u = 3f: 1/v = 1/f − 1/(3f) = 2/(3f), so **v = 1.5f.**

**Diverging lens.** A diverging lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image on the same side as the object. If its f = −12 cm and the virtual image is 5 cm from the lens (v = −5): 1/u = 1/f − 1/v = −1/12 + 1/5 = 7/60, so **u = 8.57 cm.**

**Two lenses in a line.** Find the image from lens 1, then use it as the object for lens 2, and multiply the magnifications. Object 14 cm from lens 1 (f = 10 cm): v₁ = 35 cm, m₁ = −2.5. Lens 2 (f = 7 cm) is 40 cm from lens 1, so the object distance for lens 2 is u₂ = 40 − 35 = 5 cm. Then 1/v₂ = 1/7 − 1/5 gives v₂ = −17.5 cm and m₂ = +3.5. The total magnification is **−2.5 × 3.5 = −8.75.**
keyPoints: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v; m = −v/u; converging f > 0, diverging f < 0.
u > 2f: smaller, inverted; f < u < 2f: larger, inverted; u < f: virtual, erect, magnified.
A diverging lens always gives a virtual, erect, smaller image.
Two lenses: image 1 is object 2; multiply the magnifications.

example.problem: An object 5 cm tall is placed 60 cm from a converging lens of f = 20 cm. Find the image distance and height.
example.answer: The image is real and inverted, 30 cm from the lens, and 2.5 cm tall.

exercises.prompt: An object 5 cm tall is placed 60 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. How tall is the image?
exercises.explanation: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/60 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm. m = −30/60 = −0.5, so the image height is 0.5 × 5 = 2.5 cm (inverted).
exercises.hint: Find v first, then m.

exercises.prompt: An object is placed 60 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image?
options: 30 cm from the lens, on the other side
exercises.explanation: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/60 = 2/60, so v = 30 cm (real, other side).

exercises.prompt: An object is placed in front of a converging lens so that its distance from the lens is three times the focal length. How far from the lens is the image?
exercises.hint: Write u = 3f in the equation.

exercises.prompt: For an object beyond 2f of a converging lens, the image is:
options: Diminished, inverted, and closer to the lens than the object
Magnified, inverted and farther from the lens than the object
exercises.explanation: For u > 2f the image is real, inverted and diminished, between f and 2f. It is therefore closer to the lens than the object.

exercises.prompt: The image of a pin formed by a diverging lens of focal length 12 cm is virtual and 5 cm from the lens. How far is the pin from the lens?
exercises.hint: Both f and v are negative.

exercises.prompt: When a convex lens is used as a simple magnifying glass, the object must be placed:
options: Less than one focal length from the lens
exercises.explanation: An erect, virtual, magnified image only occurs when u < f.

exercises.prompt: An object is 14 cm from a converging lens of f = 10 cm. A second converging lens of f = 7 cm is 40 cm to the right of the first. What is the magnification of the final image?
exercises.hint: The image from lens 1 is the object for lens 2.

sections.title: The lensmaker’s equation and lens power
body: **Lensmaker’s equation:** **1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂),** where R₁ and R₂ are the radii of the two surfaces (a flat surface has 1/R = 0). For a **double-convex** lens with both radii 10 cm and n = 1.52: 1/f = 0.52 × (1/10 + 1/10) = 0.104, so **f = 9.6 cm.** For a **plano-convex** lens, 1/f = (n − 1)/R, so **f = R/(n − 1).**

**Plano-convex example.** A plano-convex lens of n = 1.5 gives a virtual image with m = 3, with the image 8 cm from the lens. Virtual and magnified means v = −8 and u = 8/3 cm. Then 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 3/8 − 1/8 = 1/4, so f = 4 cm and **R = f(n − 1) = 4 × 0.5 = 2.0 cm.** For n = 1.5, m = 6 and |v| = 12 cm: u = 2 cm, 1/f = 1/2 − 1/12 = 5/12, so f = 2.4 cm, giving **R = 2.4 × 0.5 = 1.2 cm.**

**A lens in water.** The focal length depends on the index of the lens relative to its surroundings: f_water = f_air × (n − 1)/(n/n_w − 1). For a lens of n = 1.52 and f = 35 cm in air, placed in water (1.33): f_water = 35 × 0.52/(1.52/1.33 − 1) = 18.2/0.1429 = **127 cm.** A lens loses much of its power when the liquid is nearly as dense as the glass.

**Power.** The **power** of a lens is **P = 1/f** with f in metres, measured in **dioptres (D).** Converging lenses have positive power and diverging lenses negative power. For lenses placed together, **the powers add:** the eye (+60 D) with a contact lens (−10 D) gives 60 − 10 = **+50 D,** which is converging with **f = 1/50 m = 2 cm.**
keyPoints: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂); plano-convex f = R/(n − 1).
In a denser medium the focal length of a lens increases.
P = 1/f (f in m); powers of lenses in contact add.

exercises.prompt: Both radii of curvature of a double-convex lens are 10 cm and its refractive index is 1.52. What is its focal length?
exercises.explanation: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂) = 0.52 × (0.1 + 0.1) = 0.104 cm⁻¹, so f = 9.6 cm (positive, converging).
exercises.hint: Both surfaces are curved, so both terms are 1/10.

exercises.prompt: A plano-convex lens of n = 1.5 forms a virtual image with magnification 3. The image is 8 cm from the lens. What is the radius of curvature of the curved surface?
exercises.hint: Find f from the image data, then use f = R/(n − 1).

exercises.prompt: A converging lens (n = 1.52) has f = 35 cm in air. What is its focal length in water (n = 1.33)?
exercises.explanation: f_water = 35 × (1.52 − 1)/(1.52/1.33 − 1) = 18.2/0.1429 = 127 cm. In water the lens is far weaker, so the focal length increases a lot.
exercises.hint: Use the ratio of (n − 1) to (n/n_medium − 1).

exercises.prompt: A human eye of power +60 D is fitted with a contact lens of −10 D. What is the combination?
exercises.explanation: Powers add: 60 − 10 = +50 D, which is converging. f = 1/50 m = 2 cm.
exercises.hint: Add the powers, then take 1/P in metres.

sections.title: Defects of the eye
body: **The eye** focuses light onto the retina with its lens. **Short sight (myopia):** distant objects are focused in front of the retina, so the person cannot see far away. It is corrected with a **diverging (concave) lens.** **Long sight (hypermetropia):** near objects are focused behind the retina, so the person cannot see near objects clearly. It is corrected with a **converging (convex) lens.**

**Myopia worked example.** A near-sighted girl cannot see clearly beyond 25 cm. A lens must make an object at infinity look as if it is at 25 cm, on the same side: f = −25 cm = −0.25 m, so the power is **P = 1/(−0.25) = −4 D.** The power is negative because the lens is diverging.

**Near-point worked example.** A man needs a lens of f = 22 cm to read a book held 20 cm away, so the lens must form a virtual image at his near point. With u = 20 and f = 22: 1/v = 1/22 − 1/20 = −1/220, so v = −220 cm. His **near point is 220 cm** from his eye. A converging lens is the correct fix because he is long-sighted.
keyPoints: Myopia: diverging lens; hypermetropia: converging lens.
Myopia correction: f = −(far point), P = 1/f in dioptres.
Near point = |v| when the lens puts the book at u onto the near point.

exercises.prompt: Which pair correctly gives an eye defect and the lens that corrects it?
exercises.explanation: Long sight (hypermetropia) is corrected by a converging lens; short sight (myopia) needs a diverging lens.

exercises.prompt: A near-sighted girl cannot see clearly beyond 25 cm. What power of contact lens lets her see clearly at infinity?
exercises.explanation: The lens must image infinity at 25 cm: f = −0.25 m, so P = 1/f = −4 D.
exercises.hint: The lens must be diverging; use f in metres.

exercises.prompt: To read a book 20 cm away, a man needs a lens of focal length 22 cm. What is his near point?
exercises.explanation: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/22 − 1/20 = −1/220, so v = −220 cm. The virtual image is at his near point, 220 cm away.
exercises.hint: The image is virtual, so v is negative; the near point is |v|.

sections.title: Prisms, dispersion and achromatic lenses
body: **Minimum deviation.** For a prism of apex angle A and index n, at minimum deviation D: **n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2).** Rearranged, **D = 2 sin⁻¹(n sin(A/2)) − A.** For A = 65° and n = 1.75, D = **75.2°.** If the angle of minimum deviation equals the apex angle (D = A), then n = sin A / sin(A/2) = 2 cos(A/2), so for n = 1.55 the apex angle is A = **78.38°.**

**Dispersion** happens because n depends on colour: violet is bent more than red. With A = 60°, red (n = 1.61) has D = 47.2° and violet (n = 1.66) has D = 52.2°, so the difference is about **5°.** For a **thin prism** the deviation is **D = (n − 1)A,** so the angle of dispersion is **(n_v − n_r)A.** A 20° thin prism with n_v = 1.6434 and n_r = 1.6648 gives (1.6648 − 1.6434) × 20 = **0.43°.**

**Achromatic doublet.** A converging lens of crown glass and a diverging lens of flint glass in contact can cancel the colour fringes. The condition is **ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0,** where ω is the dispersive power of each glass. The combined focal length obeys **1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂.** An object at 20 cm that gives a real image at 30 cm shows f = 12 cm. With ω₁:ω₂ = 2:3, the conditions give **f₁ = 4 cm and f₂ = −6 cm:** check 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 and 2/4 + 3/(−6) = 0.
keyPoints: n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2) at minimum deviation.
Dispersion: violet bends more than red; thin prism D = (n − 1)A.
Achromatic doublet: ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0 and 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂.

exercises.prompt: A prism has an apex angle of 65° and is made of material of index 1.75. What is the angle of minimum deviation?
exercises.hint: Use half of the apex angle inside the sine.

exercises.prompt: A glass prism of n = 1.55 is built so that its angle of minimum deviation equals its apex angle. What is the apex angle?
exercises.explanation: If D = A then n = sin A/sin(A/2) = 2cos(A/2), so cos(A/2) = 0.775 and A/2 = 39.19°, so A = 78.38°.
exercises.hint: Use the double-angle identity sin A = 2 sin(A/2) cos(A/2).

exercises.prompt: A glass prism has n = 1.61 for red and 1.66 for violet. Light passes symmetrically through its 60° apex angle. What is the difference in deviation between the colours?
exercises.hint: Compute the deviation for each colour, then subtract.

exercises.prompt: A thin glass prism has apex angle 20°, n_violet = 1.6434 and n_red = 1.6648. What is the angle of dispersion?
exercises.hint: For a thin prism D = (n − 1)A.

exercises.prompt: An object 20 cm from an achromatic doublet gives a real image 30 cm from it. The dispersive powers of the two glasses are in the ratio 2:3. What are the focal lengths of the two lenses?
exercises.explanation: 1/f = 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12, so f = 12 cm. The achromatic condition ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0 with 2:3 gives f₂ = −1.5f₁, and 1/f₁ − 1/(1.5f₁) = 1/(3f₁) = 1/12 gives f₁ = 4 cm and f₂ = −6 cm.
exercises.hint: The condition uses the powers (1/f), not the focal lengths.

exercises.prompt: Which statements are true? (i) Optical density relates to how much a medium slows the transmission of light. (ii) In reflection, energy is not conserved. (iii) At a perfect reflector there is no refraction.
exercises.explanation: (i) is true, and (iii) is true because all the light is reflected. (ii) is false: reflection conserves energy.
